blocks.html: Introduction

I investigate how Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) prices are affected by interstate trading of RECs. A REC is a commodity representing the ownership right to one MWh of renewable power. By understanding how interstate supply and demand changes impact REC prices, we may better establish the basic economic theory of how a REC is priced in the context of a larger trading environment. The paper is ordered as follows: first, I introduce the Renewable Portfolio Standard regulation that sets the structure of the REC market. Then, I explore the current limitations in the available literature, delineating how the theory must be expanded to include regional trade in light of recent price behavior of RECs. Subsequently, I will establish a microeconomic model that incorporates such trade, characterizing equilibrium and exploring implications of the model. I will confirm the model’s strength with data from the PJM interconnection area—which administers, manages, and operates the wholesale electricity market and REC tracking system for the eastern Midwest and Mid-Atlantic states—by employing two different regression specifications to test the veracity of the two main implications of the model. Finally, I will conceptually and briefly discuss potential policy ideas that may decrease volatility and stabilize prices across the region, then conclude the paper.

Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) have been enacted in thirty states and the District of Columbia, mandating that a certain percentage of electricity supply from in-state electricity providers (utilities) come from renewable sources. Given the difficulty in tracking actual electricity flows, to track and ensure compliance by providers, states have created renewable energy certificate (REC) programs. As stated, each REC is a tradeable commodity representing one MWh of renewable energy generated, and can either be sold along with the physical power (a bundled REC) or separately as a derivative representing the ownership right to that renewable power (an unbundled REC). To comply with a state’s RPS, each electricity provider in each state acquires a certain number of unbundled or bundled RECs (depending on state regulation) by bilaterally purchasing from renewable electricity generators or buying them on secondary markets from each other, and subsequently submits the required amount for compliance each year to the state’s energy regulation authority. Such policies have been increasingly adopted by states as foundational environmental policy across the United States, as they are thought to increase a state’s renewable energy production and mitigate climate change through decreasing emissions from fossil fuel-based energy. However, a lack of clarity emerges on the overarching supply, demand, and price characteristics of RECs due to a disjointed policy design and market structure, which I will outline below, contributing to high price volatility and unexpected changes in one state’s REC prices due to the policy changes of another state.

RPS goals and targets are different across states, targeting varying objectives. However, a somewhat standardized market to track the amount of renewable energy certificates generated, bought, and sold across states gives us the chance to explore heterogeneous RPS policy treatments across states on equilibrium REC prices. Because electricity providers must redeem a certain number of RECs into the state’s energy regulation authority to comply with the state government’s renewable portfolio standard each year, a captive market exists where, as stated, electricity providers buy certificates directly from an extremely limited set of utility-scale renewable energy generators, as well as buy and sell them to each other on a secondary market, where supply is again limited.

A single REC may be traded, provided that (1) the buyer finds some useful value in it, which is almost always in RPS compliance, (2) it has been certified in at least one state as generated by a RPS-eligible renewable generator, and (3) it has not been previously retired for compliance in a state. If the necessary amount of RECs are not submitted by a utility for RPS compliance, it must pay an alternative compliance payment (ACP) per REC of non-compliance to the state, an amount pre-determined by state regulation. Thus, the ACP can be thought of as a substitute good with a single price to the REC, as it fulfills the exact same function: RPS compliance. As a result, the price of any state’s traded REC in a state would conceivably be below that state’s ACP, acting as a price cap, since an electricity provider would simply pay the ACP rather than buy a REC that is selling above that price. The demand curve for a REC in a single state can then be approximated by a transition from perfectly elastic to perfectly inelastic: a provider is a price taker of RECs until it fulfills its RPS compliance quantity, then immediately demands zero of the commodity, as it no longer has any utility to derive from it. Thus, beyond the mandated quantity, the price will be nearly $0 because there is almost no other need for RECs.2 Below this quantity, the price will nearly be at the price ceiling equal to the ACP, as any price even slightly below the ACP will be economically beneficial for the provider. In the short-run (i.e. in a given year), the supply of RECs is thought to be essentially fixed without any elasticity, as renewable generators do not typically choose to generate/not generate based on price of RECs. If the sun is shining, a solar farm will generate RECs, and if the wind is blowing, a wind farm will generate RECs, regardless of price. Thus, while supply may vary stochastically with the weather, it is vertical in the short-run for a state. Thus, such a supply-demand model is illustrated in Figure 1.

blocks.html: Limitations of Current Theory

However, recent events have thrown this model with a theoretical “price cap”, signified by the ACP, into doubt. Specifically, in 2023, Maryland’s RECs have been trading at around $34, which is $4 greater than its ACP of $30 (see Figure 2). Under the current model, this price should not be possible, yet the price has not only gone over this theoretical limit, but has also been steadily increasing in the past year. Such a dramatic price increase and the unexpected violation of theory has accompanied increases in demand and changes in policy structure outside Maryland, indicating that out-of-state effects and interstate REC trading is affecting the price of a state’s RECs, even though that state itself has not greatly changed factors affecting supply, demand, or consumer/producer expectations. Additionally, the increase in price has not been gradual or slow, and has exhibited the characteristic volatility of REC markets, with +20% swings in price. Given this unprecedented behavior, a new model, incorporating regional demand (not just state-specific demand) and interstate trading of RECs, seems very much necessary.

blocks.html: In the existing literature, there are very few papers that analyze the effects of interstate trading on RECs. One of the first mathematical models for a REC Market is proposed by Marchenko (2008), in which the maximum price is similarly given by the fine a utility pays for non-compliance (see Figure 3).

More recently, Coulon, Khazaei, and Powell (2015) do propose a stochastic pricing model that attempts to account for market rules in predicting prices for the New Jersey Solar REC market (a “carve-out” of the RPS that requires a smaller percentage of a provider’s electricity supply to come from specifically solar generation), which have historically exhibited extreme volatility, ranging from nearly $0 to the state’s Solar ACP of $500. While the paper successfully recreates historical price movements in the NJ Solar REC (SREC) Market, it must be noted that such SREC markets are essentially siloed to each state. Regulations for SREC carve-outs in states typically require that the SREC is generated by an in-state generator, i.e. New Jersey cannot obtain an out-of-state-generated SREC to fulfill its Solar RPS compliance. Thus, cross-state demand of SRECs typically is not present, and so the supply-demand framework in which the paper works is the one proposed by Marchenko (2008).

Yet, this framework does not explain the recent behavior exhibited by Maryland RECs.

blocks.html: Baamonde-Seoane et al. (2021), Khazaei, Coulon, and Powell (2017), and Hustveit, Frogner, and Fleten (2017) also build upon the stochastic model of Coulon, Khazaei, and Powell (2015). Specifically, Baamonde-Seoane et al. (2021) extends the model to a more statistically rigorous framework, assuming that the price of a REC depends on “two stochastic factors. More precisely, these factors are the renewable generation rate and the number of accumulated green certificates.” Hustveit, Frogner, and Fleten (2017) considers the Swedish–Norwegian electricity certificate market, and by using a similar stochastic model based on dynamic programming, conclude that “prices are highly sensitive to changes in electricity consumption and generation.” Yet, the Swedish–Norwegian electricity certificate market again exhibits the “cliff”-shaped demand curve, as there is a single federal policy that sets a single ACP. Khazaei, Coulon, and Powell (2017) also proposes a penalty policy that creates a sloped demand curve to combat extreme price volatility, but still does not account for the effects of cross-state trading and demand that may more intensely affect price dynamics. Thus, it is clear that interstate trading must be accounted for if we are to explain recent REC price behavior, and my paper aims to add to the literature in two specific ways in this context: (1) to build a theoretical microeconomic model that adequately accounts for the possibility of trading and the subsequent price behaviors that have been exhibited in regions like PJM where prices exceed a state’s ACP and (2) to validate the theorized price determinants and expected trading behavior of market participants (i.e. which states are exporters/importers) within that theoretical framework via empirical data.
REC Market Trading

Logistically, ownership and issuance of RECs are tracked in standardized regional registries such as the PJM Interconnection authority’s Generation Attribute Tracking System (known as PJM-GATS, which tracks certificates for DC, DE, IL, MD, NJ, OH, PA, and VA). However, while RECs are tracked in a single system, all RECs cannot be used in a universal manner.

Particularly, each state constructs their RPS policy to meet their respective goals, such as grid diversity, economic growth, technology-focused build-out, usage of state-abundant renewable resource endowments, and other state-specific preferences and focuses. Because of this variance in policy purpose, scope, implementation, and design across states, each state places geographical limits which generator’s RECs can be used for compliance in their state. For example, Illinois requires all RECs submitted for compliance with the state’s RPS to come from generators that are physically located in Illinois, while New Jersey allows any RECs that are “generated within or delivered into the PJM region” to be submitted for compliance with its RPS program. As a result, a New Jersey electricity provider may obtain its RECs for RPS compliance from an Illinois-located generator, while an Illinois electricity provider cannot obtain RECs for its RPS compliance from a New Jersey. As such, the price of an Illinois REC (called an IL Renewable Credit) can be affected by out-of-state demand, and potentially push it above the in-state ACP level, provided there is large enough out-of-state demand from providers who are willing to pay for that IL Renewable Credit above Illinois’ ACP.

Simply put, only generators that generate RECs certified or deemed eligible by the state government can be used by a utility to meet its RPS compliance. The entrance of the generator into a registry like PJM-GATS only happens after certification, and any RECs produced by the generator is issued by the registry thereafter. Thus, if a renewable generator generates RECs while located in a state with a low ACP, but its RECs can be used for a provider’s RPS compliance in another state with a high ACP, it is economically beneficial for that generator to export its RECs to another state’s provider to claim a higher price, since the out-of-state utility is subject to a higher ACP. It is the out-of-state utility’s responsibility to ensure that the RPS it is subject to allows out-of-state-generated RECs to be submitted for its compliance. Thus, interstate trading of RECs happens under the following conditions:

In a given region, there are at least some electricity providers that may fulfill their home state’s RPS compliance by submitting RECs that have been generated out-of-state.

In a given region, there are varying RPS requirements that set different quantities of RECs that must be demanded, meaning that any shortage or surplus of RECs for one state may be adjusted for by exporting/importing RECs to/from a different state.

Price volatility is also then explained not only by supply-side factors as the current literature theorizes, but also by any changes in the above factors in a larger trading paradigm. To illustrate this more concretely, I look at the PJM region as a case study—specifically the REC trade relationship between Maryland and Virginia—to understand how the three above factors are shifting both REC prices and REC export/import behaviors of suppliers/utilities for states with mandatory RPS regulation. For the next section and the rest of this paper, I will only focus on the market of Tier I or Class I RECs, which are the highest class/tier of RECs from a ranking system based on lowest environmental impact and includes main renewable technologies like solar, wind, geothermal, biomass, and fuel cells.
REC Trading: Maryland and Virginia

The case of Maryland and Virginia are particularly interesting with regards to recent REC trading & price trends. As stated in the introduction, Maryland has recently experienced the anomaly of having its RECs priced above its theoretical price cap set by the state ACP. This price behavior becomes interesting when considered in the context of Virginia’s recent entry into the mandatory REC market. Specifically, up to 2020, Virginia had a voluntary RPS in place, which is an RPS that incentivizes utilities for meeting its REC target but does not penalize the utility for each REC of noncompliance, as a mandatory RPS program (like Maryland’s) would. Yet, it had still been supplying RECs to the PJM region; thus, its entrance into the market can be thought of as solely impacting demand, giving us the opportunity to understand how a demand shock in the form of a new market participant affects REC trade and pricing for another state in the market who has not altered any of its behavior.

As one of the earliest states to adopt an RPS with fairly aggressive targets, Maryland utilities has steadily increased its imports of RECs and has maintained its status as a net importer of RECs for the past decade and a half. Its RPS states that “Source of RECs must be (1) located in the PJM Region; or (2) outside the area described in item (1) but in a control area that is adjacent to the PJM service territory, if the electricity is delivered into the PJM service territory.” On the other hand, given the lack of REC utility for Virginia utilities until 2020, generators in Virginia had been steadily increasing its export of RECs into other states, as they could sell for higher prices in those states (such as Maryland). The evolution of these net exports, along with Virginia and Maryland’s ACP and RPS requirement (as a percentage of electricity supply) is shown in Table 1.

As stated, before 2021, Virginia was under a voluntary regime. Thus, while the state was a supplier of RECs to the larger PJM market (states with mandatory RPS could buy Virginia-generated RECs to fulfill their RPS requirement), the state’s utilities demanded very few RECs from the mandatory market, making the state a heavy net exporter of RECs. Thus, it makes sense that in Figure 4 we see that most of the RECs submitted to this voluntary program (2019 and 2020) were domestically created. However, once the Virginia state government enacts the mandatory RPS in 2020, we see that Virginia’s utilities immediately begins to import RECs, most notably from PA, MD, and NJ. This shift in importing behavior subsequently coincides with a very sharp and immediate increase in REC prices for those states (some time lag in the price response is expected for the demand shock to be observed in its entirety). As such, it is clear that we need a model accounting for the possibility of REC trading; only then can we explain the seemingly anomalous shifts in prices and importing behavior by states’ utilities that result from shocks to the market that impact the demand and price for out-of-state RECs. The current literature does not account for how prices and trade for a given state may be directly affected by the behavioral changes of out-of-state generators and out-of-state utilities.

The Model: A Trading Paradigm

The goal of this paper is simple in principle: to create a new supply-demand model that adequately accounts for the possibility of REC trade within a region of states while capturing the empirical phenomena that have been recently observed in REC markets. Namely, by accounting for the possibility of trade we should be able to also capture three characteristics of the REC market (1) the potential for a state’s REC price to break through its ACP, (2) extreme price volatility, and (3) changes in export/import behavior of a state from out-of-state demand and supply shocks. Such a model is built below.
The Demand Function

Given that the system of RPS’s in a given region establishes varying price caps, required quantities, and eligibility rules in buying RECs, conceptualizing a new demand curve is the first task at hand. Instead of a single “cliff” demand curve that has been long assumed in the literature, the demand function in a trading environment can be now represented by a decreasing staircase function of combined cliffs, with each “step” sub-area representing the demand of a single state in the trading region as a function of price. The Supply Function

As established in previous literature, the supply function is dependent mostly on two factors: the generation of renewable energy and the amount of banked certificates. For the sake of both simplicity and specifically understanding the impact of trading on REC prices, I will ignore the banking effects on supply, which are thought to be small in the first place. The generation of renewable energy, however, is dependent on two additional factors, the first of which affects supply in the short-run and the second of which affects supply in the long-run. Thus, depending on the amount of time considered, our supply varies as follows:

Short-Run Supply: Weather and Climate Factors. Existing renewable energy generators cannot choose, in the normal economic sense, when to produce RECs, because the generation process is dependent on weather conditions, which is an exogenously-given, stochastic variable (the amount of sunshine or the amount of wind that blows is modeled as a random variable). Thus, in a sense, a renewable energy generator is always operating at “full capacity,” unless a generator chooses to shut down entirely. Again, for the sake of simplicity in the model, I assume that REC generators cannot hold onto and store RECs before selling them, meaning that they cannot speculate to potentially sell them at a higher price. Thus, in the short-term, the price of RECs has a negligible impact on the number of RECs supplied to the market. Assuming a small impact of operational costs (i.e. workers to run/clean generators, maintenance, etc.), the supply function will thus be very inelastic in the short-run. I will approximate this via a perfectly inelastic supply function (i.e. fixed generation).

Long-Run Supply: Buildout of Renewable Energy Generation. In the long-run, we will observe an upward sloping supply curve, due to the fact that more renewable generators can choose to enter the market at higher prices and increase the quantity of RECs supplied. Entrance into the market, however, takes a very long time due to barriers to entry and long construction times. Normally, a utility-scale solar generator farm that can generate a significant amount of RECs take around 12-24 months to develop and construct, while a utility-scale wind generator farm can take up to 3-4 years to develop and construct (sometimes longer), and firms will build more and more of these generators in the long-run as the price of RECs increase. While buildout is kept fixed in the short-run and generation is thus fixed, in the long-run, there is scope for buildout to vary. Thus, in the long-run, supply can be approximated by a linear function that is more elastic than in the short-run case.

In a trading framework, the implications of the above description are twofold for a given year : (1) that the supply of RECs in a trading region in the short-run is given by the sum of RECs generated over all the states in the trading region, meaning that weather conditions/maintenance and operations costs in one state will shift the supply for the entire region and (2) that in the long-run, the aggressive investment into renewable energy generation build-out via an incentive program by any one state in the trading region can lead to a supply shock that affects prices for all states in the region. However, for this paper, I will be focusing on how states are meeting their RPS mandate in a single year, which narrows our consideration of supply to the short-run. As such, the above descriptive formulation for the short-run supply can be formalized into a supply function as follows. It is easy to construct, as supply is inelastic:

Applying the Model: A Theoretical Scenario

Before moving onto the data, I first admit that the above model is quite notationally dense. This is due to the fact that the demand function is a “step function” and needs to be discretely defined via intervals and sums rather than via a smooth, differentiable function across the entire domain. Thus, it would be prudent to concretize the above formalisms with a simple example consisting of a trading region with three states, as follows.

Supply Shock

Perhaps the most pertinent shock to consider in our model would be REC supply shocks. Given recent efforts, both at the state and federal level, to aggressively expand the buildout of renewable energy generation, the supply of RECs will most likely skyrocket in the coming years (if currently planned legislation passes and existing legislation is not repealed). In the context of our model, this means that . Once again, to better concretize this, let us return to our three-state example with = 3.

We originally stated that the total supply in region in year is given by = 1000+300+150 = 1400 RECs. However, let us imagine that state A recently passed an aggressive legislative agenda that seeks to accelerate approval and construction of solar farms, in order to increase the supply of RECs generated in their state by 70% in the next 12 months. Thus, if all goes according to plan, state A’s supply of RECs should go from = 1000 = 1700. State B and C do not pass any additional legislation, and, for the sake of simplicity, let us assume that all three states keep their RPS compliance quantities constant from to +1. Then, we have that supply increased from = 1000 + 300 + 100 = 1400 to = 1700 + 300 + 100 = 2100. However we notice that this supply is greater than any quantity demanded:

Thus, state A’s policy has pushed the supply of RECs in the region into an oversupply, where more RECs exist than demanded by regulation. This means that, if there are no shocks to demand from to + 1, the equilibrium price of RECs are essentially zero, or = 0. This is an intuitive general result, as we would expect any abundantly available commodity with an oversupply will carry an essentially zero price if demand is fixed, as in the case of RECs. However, there is another important interpretation here at hand here: given that many renewable energy generators depend on RECs to make up the difference between the cost of generating fossil fuel-based energy and renewable energy, as buildout continues, there is a price cannibalization effect that decreases the attractiveness of investment into renewable energy due to the decrease in REC prices. This, of course, assumes that energy demand and consumption in general stays the same and that renewable generators will not benefit from any increase in wholesale electricity prices. Nevertheless, it is important that, in the context of our trading model, just one state’s aggressive investment into renewable energy generation may impact the profitability and buildout of renewable projects in other states.
Demand Shock

Now, let us imagine that there is a demand shock in the form of amended RPS regulation for a state in region . This is also quite common; over the past decade, as more and more states commit to more renewable generation in their energy mix, they have amended their originally enacted RPS policies to reflect more aggressive goals. The most aggressive example is Rhode Island in 2022, which updated its RPS goal to 100% of energy generation by 2033. A demand shock can come in forms other than just amendment of the REC requirements; states like Massachusetts have made their ACP higher to reflect more stringent penalties, and a state who previously did not have a mandatory RPS can create a large demand shock in the market by enacting one and subsequently joining a trading region (more on this in Section 5). An out-of-state demand shock that significantly increases demand for RECs in the entire trading region may explain how a state’s generators might be selling its RECs at a price that is above that state’s ACP. This scenario is likely a big part of the explanation as to why Maryland’s RECs are trading at a price that is higher than its ACP — because other states are increasing demand for Maryland’s RECs through their state policies, even though Maryland has not adjusted any of its policies. Such interstate impact is possible because of the trade that happens between states—an impact that has been long overlooked in previous literature on REC pricing.
Implications of the Model within the Example

Now that we have built a supply and demand model and characterized equilibrium in that model, we will seek to understand the theoretical implications of the model we have built in the context of the above scenario. By using our example scenario, we will be able to gain better intuition about the implications of model and thus better confirm whether those implications can adequately account for and explain empirical phenomena in a real REC market in Section 5.
Price Implications

The most evident (and somewhat trivial) implication is that in our model, all market participants should be paying a single price for RECs, given the demand and supply is aggregated across all the states. In the context of our example, states A, B, and C should all be paying a single price for RECs, since supply and demand are aggregated across all three states. Price volatility should then be accounted for by supply shocks or demand shocks as stated in the two previous subsections. In this respect, a demand/supply shock affecting any one state should impact the REC prices for all the states in the trading region. This is an important implication for policymakers to consider—no matter how well-designed the RPS is to keep REC prices low, any shock to any state in the region could potentially affect REC prices for all utilities and generators in the region, whichever state they might be in. Thus, the incorporation of trade into a REC market impacts the effectiveness of the RPS, both in terms of focused renewable generation buildout in a state and any state-specific targets that a legislature might have had in mind when passing the RPS. The cross-state effects of trading might dampen or augment these state-specific goals, and policymakers must be aware of this when making any amendments to the RPS.
Trading Implications

Perhaps less evident, but still equally as important of an implication, is the implied trade flows between states in the context of this model. Given that different states in the region differ in their willingness to pay for the RECs, we should see that generators (suppliers) from low-ACP states exporting their RECs and selling them to out-of-state utilities (consumers). Specifically, if the price of a REC in trading region is clearing at a price that is higher than state ’s ACP, we should be seeing that state C is exporting its RECs to utilities subject to RPS regulation in states B and A, since state C’s utilities has no incentive to pay for RECs at a price higher than their ACP. For example, if the equilibrium quantity in regions is set such that the equilibrium price is = $30, then utilities in state C would much rather pay their ACP of $20 than pay $30 for a REC. Thus, generators in state C, rather than selling to utilities in state C, will look to utilities in states B and A, whose ACPs are equal or higher than the current trading price and will be willing to pay that equilibrium for state C’s RECs (assuming that states B and A can use state C’s RECs for RPS compliance). State C should then either be paying the ACP to fulfill its RPS requirement or procuring them from states with voluntary RPS/no RPS, since those states will value their own RECs at a near-zero price. In this respect, when aggregating the data on ACP and net exports across all of the region’s states states’ net exports should be decreasing in the states’ ACPs.

This implication also tells us that RPS policies do not only have localized effects; policy enactments and amendments may have large impacts on other states’ RPS compliance and REC procurement behavior. Specifically, there will be a group of net importers and net exporters; the former would be those with ACPs that are higher than the current market equilibrium price, and the latter would be those with ACPs lower than the equilibrium price. Such an implication matches up with the trading relationship between Maryland and Virginia as delineated in Section ??: Maryland’s exports increased dramatically when Virginia joined the PJM REC market and caused the price of Maryland RECs to increase dramatically due to the positive demand shock, while Virginia’s imports increase dramatically as its ACP went from below the market clearing price to above it. Thus, more generally, we can hypothesize that if there is a demand or supply shock in the REC market that affects price, the implications of our model tell us that we should see the following changes in flows:

If a demand or supply shock leads to an decrease in equilibrium price, such that the price is now lower than the ACP of a former net exporter state, we should see that state’s utilities (buyers) change their trading behavior to take advantage of the new equilibrium price that is now lower than its ACP by importing more RECs from lower ACP states.

If a demand or supply shock leads to an increase in equilibrium price, such that the price is now higher than the ACP of a former net importer state, we should see that state’s generators (suppliers) change their trading behavior to take advantage of the new equilibrium price that is now higher than its ACP by exporting more RECs to higher ACP states.

The intuition here is that, if a state’s generators are not constrained to sell their RECs in their home state and utilities with a higher willingness to pay exist in other states, they will choose to sell into whichever state maximizes profit. Similarly, if not constrained by policy to do so, utilities will choose whichever state’s RECs are cheaper and meets requirements, rather than obtaining RECs from their home state.

These trade flows also imply that the RPS may not be accomplishing its goal in full: if utilities are choosing to obtain RECs from other states rather than their own states’ generators due to high ACPs and unreasonably lofty RPS requirements, there will be more buildout of renewables out-of-state from this increased demand rather than in-state, which runs counter to the goals of a state’s RPS. As states import more RECs rather than generate them in-state, there may be a possibility that “hubs” of renewable energy generation will arise, where generators will simply get built in states with favorable renewable resource endowments, favorable regulatory environments, and low development costs, rather than incentivizing renewable generation within the specific state that the RPS in enacted in. This result might be favorable for federal policy, but if a state government’s goal is to spur generation of RECs and renewables in their own state, the participation in a trading environment with an aggregated market seems to weaken the strength of the RPS policy.

In the next section, I seek to confirm these implications with empirical evidence from the PJM trading region, which covers much of the Mid-Atlantic and Eastern Midwest states. Specifically, I will first use price data to verify that supply and demand shocks to the region are accompanied by price movements similar to what I have theorized in the model, then also corroborate the model’s predicted movements in trade inflows/outflows with REC export/import data.
Testing the Model: The PJM Region
To recap, I seek to confirm the following two implications present in our model:

REC price behavior should be volatile given the characterization of equilibrium in Section 3 and essentially equal among states that can freely trade. REC prices should thus change equally for all states in a trading region if there is a demand or supply shock brought by even one state.

There should be a group of net importers and net exporters each year, based on the equilibrium price; namely, those states with ACPs above the equilibrium price should be net importers, while those states with ACPs below the equilibrium price should be net exporters. As a result, net exports (exports - imports) should be decreasing as ACP of a state increases. Moreover, trade flows should adjust accordingly in response to any demand or supply shock that impacts REC prices for the region, as delineated in Section 2.

I use data from the PJM interconnection region, as it is one of the more established trading regions for RECs with an active REC trade market for the past fifteen years. It also has a good mix of states with varying ACPs and different RPS targets. As a result, the region has many publicly available datasets on RECs for usage, stored by both the PJM Interconnection Authority and private vendors who open trading platforms for RECs. The PJM region tracks all of its RECs in its environmental services arm, called the PJM Region Environmental Information Services (PJM-EIS). This sub-organization within the PJM Interconnection authority also manages the Generation Attribute Tracking System (GATS) in which generators within the region can register their RECs and have them officially certified by states. Thus, our data comes from two sources. The price data comes from a private brokerage, Evolution Markets, which establishes a platform for REC trading, and the REC trade balance data comes from the PJM-EIS’s public GATS report on both the state of origin and the state of retirement of RECs for all RECs retired in a reporting year in the PJM region.

But this is not the case on closer analysis of the data and regulations for D.C. and Ohio as well as the characteristics associated with the PJM tri-qualified RECs.

Specifically, D.C. did not produce any RECs until 2018; thus, the price of D.C. RECs were essentially zero until this time, as shown in plot 2 of Figure 9, because there were none to buy. Thus, this affects the coefficient on both PJM average price and non-PJM average price, since D.C. was essentially only importing and not exporting any RECs until 2018; thus D.C. RECs were not able to be priced until then. Moreover, Ohio has a complex RPS in which utilities are only allowed to acquire RECs that have been produced within or adjacent to the state of Ohio, and usually cannot obtain RECs from the wider PJM region, although its generators still can supply RECs to the rest of the region. However, this requirement in Ohio that utilities must meet compliance with in-state RECs means that the supply of Ohio-generated RECs are mostly being used by Ohio utilities for compliance. This further means that RECs produced from what would be considered “Tier I” or “Class I” sources (i.e. solar, wind, geothermal, fuel cells, biomass, as mentioned in Section 1) that are valuable to non-Ohio utilities are being used for compliance by Ohio utilities first before being available for trade. Thus, the Ohio-generated RECs that are available for import by other states are generated from lesser technologies and sometimes cannot be used for “Tier I” RPS compliance. Hence, they are valued at a lower price by other PJM states, which explains why movements in average PJM Tier I prices does not have the initially expected 1-to-1 impact on Ohio RECs. Essentially, the Ohio-generated RECs that are available for trade are not part of the same shared market that is shown for the other states in Figure 9. And, as mentioned in the caption for Figure 9, PJM tri-qualified RECs carry inherently more valuable characteristics for utilities that provide power across state lines, which raises their prices by a small factor. Thus, it is reasonable to expect that shifts in price for the wider region would have a slightly more than 1-to-1 impact on these tri-qualified RECs.

Thus, the regression above establishes strong evidence for the fact that the model is an apt description of price behavior for a trading region in which the states may freely trade RECs with each other. I have confirmed that (1) states are essentially paying a single price for RECs in the PJM region (controlling for slight characteristic differences in the RECs themselves) and (2) any shifts in or shocks to price for any PJM state affects every state’s price equally, as shown by 1 for the states that trade similar RECs, as our model in Section 3 implies. As ancillary evidence, I have also shown in the regression that any shocks and movements in REC prices outside of our considered PJM trading region, like the NEPOOL region, does not affect PJM prices ( 0), as their RPS/ACPs would not be a part of the demand and supply functions constructed in Section 3. Hence, empirical evidence supports the strength of my model in understanding and predicting price dynamics for a REC trading region, like PJM.
Trade Flows

REC trade in the PJM region has been increasing dramatically in the past few years (as seen in Figure 8) due to the standardization of which RECs can count towards a state’s RPS. Specifically, many states in the region have now begun to accept any RECs generated within the PJM region as eligible for their state’s RPS compliance. The increase in imports is especially notable in states like Maryland and Virginia, whose RPS requirements have increased rapidly in the past few years.

I seek to now empirically confirm the second implication of my model. Namely, in a larger trading paradigm, given that the demand function for the whole region is a function of states’ (1) ACP (willingness to pay) and (2) RPS-required REC quantity (quantity demanded), we should see that net exports are increasing (i.e. more exports) when both of these price determinants decrease. More intuitively put, states with lower ACPs should be exporting many more RECs to take advantage of utilities that are willing to pay more for RECs, while states with higher ACPs should be importing many more RECs to take advantage of RECs selling more cheaply than their ACPs. blocks.html: Conclusion

This paper has analyzed the current REC pricing literature and identified recent empirical trends that have shown the limitations of current theory, subsequently proposing a new pricing framework that incorporates trade amongst multiple states with RPS regulation. There are two main implications that arise from this new model that I propose, one regarding state-by-state REC pricing behavior in response to shocks, one regarding shifts in trading behavior by the market participants. The implications are confirmed using data from the PJM region, showing that the newly built model adequately accounts for recent, anomalous empirical trends in the PJM REC market.

I find that, when accounting for interstate trading of RECs, supply is given inelastically as explored previously in the literature and the demand function for the region dependent on two factors: the ACPs of the states in the region and each state’s RPS-mandated REC requirement. Thus, with demand being approximated by a step function, equilibrium prices will not always be uniquely determined, exacerbating price volatility. The model also implies that REC prices for different states will be equal or similar, an implication that is confirmed via empirical analysis from the PJM region.

From this model, I establish two main implications that I confirm with data from the PJM region: (1) REC prices should be roughly equalized across states in the trading region such that movements and shocks to REC price in any state(s) in the region should produce an equal movement for all other state REC prices in the region and (2) that certain states should be importing large quantities of RECs, while some states should be exporting large quantities of RECs, depending on whether their ACP is high (importer) or low (exporter). I empirically confirm these two main implications via regressions as specified in Section 5.

Before I conclude, I would like to briefly consider two policy discussions. Given this model and its implications, it is clear that there are two immediate policy adjustments that could be made to decrease price volatility and spur greater renewable buildout. First, a region like PJM could equalize the ACP across all the states, essentially removing the dependence of the demand function on multiple ACPs such that the willingness to pay for all states is unified. Then, all market participants (states) would be price takers, and full compliance with RPS’s for all states in the region would depend solely on whether supply can match the RPS-mandated REC requirement. There would be no trade, as generators are no longer incentivized to export RECs, nor are utilities incentivized to import RECs, since the maximum willingness to pay is equalized; generators would simply sell RECs to their respective states’ utilities (i.e. nearly all REC transactions would be confined to the state’s borders). Second, a federalized trading system for RECs could be considered, in which each state keeps their respective ACPs and RPS-mandated REC requirements, but all states with RPS’s can trade RECs with one another, unconstrained by regulation that deems RECs generated in certain states/regions to be eligible for submission. With such a centralized trading platform, the demand function as specified in Section 3 would have fifty ACPs and fifty RPS’s setting each state’s demand; thus, shocks to demand and supply would have a much weaker effect on the price, thereby decreasing price volatility for all states with RPS regulation. By making federal trade of RECs available, one would essentially add more “steps” to the demand curve as depicted in Figure 6, and thus, the equilibrium price “jumping” to a new step would be a much smaller transition than in a region with a few states (like PJM). While I do not pursue this discussion more rigorously in this paper, it is certainly an area for future research to take place.

In any case, with this new model, both traders of RECs and policymakers designing RPS regulation may better predict how shocks to the market and changes to regulatory frameworks may affect the larger REC market. More specifically, states can understand how regulatory changes in a different state that is in the same trading region may impact its REC prices, while buyers and traders of RECs may better adjust expectations for future REC prices and shifts in trading behavior by market participants within my proposed framework. While there are many more implications and questions that arise as a result of this framework and more sophisticated mathematical methods can be used within this framework to establish more precise theory (i.e. dynamical programming methods to determine the utilities/generators optimization problems, characterization of equilibria in the long-term, how banking/storage of RECs impacts this model), I believe that this framework sets a solid foundation for future research in the many of the topics I have briefly touched upon in this paper.

abstract: I study the price behavior of Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) in a trading environment to account for recent empirical observations that have exposed limitations in current theory. I develop first a novel supply-demand model that characterizes equilibrium for the market and detail the implications of that model, showing that a state’s REC prices and trade flows may be affected by out-of-state shocks and regulation. I then empirically confirm this model with data from the regional PJM REC market, focusing on the model’s aforementioned implications for price dynamics and trade flows. I find that this model suitably accounts for recent empirical observations of REC prices breaking above their theorized price cap (which is set by state RPS regulation as a penalty for each REC of noncompliance) and explains how regulatory changes for and shocks to any one market participant induces equally large price shifts and trading behavior adjustments for all market participants.1
